entries.question: Who owns the earth?
entries.books_in_tension: Genesis, Exodus, Deuteronomy, 1 Chronicles, Psalms, Matthew, Luke, 1 Corinthians
entries.summary: A wide set of passages (Gen 14:19, 22; Exod 9:29; 19:5; Deut 10:14; Ps 24:1; 50:12; 89:11; 1 Cor 10:26) affirm that God owns the earth absolutely. Matthew 4:8-9 and Luke 4:5-6 have Satan offer all the kingdoms of the world to Jesus — an offer only meaningful if Satan has them to give. Psalm 115:16 complicates the picture further by saying the earth has been given to 'the children of men.'
entries.commentary: This is a three-way contradiction and it's best handled structurally rather than as a binary. On the God-ownership side, the claim is ontological: God is creator and therefore proprietor. Apologists like Walton and Carson argue the Satan passages and Psalm 115 operate at a different register — Satan is the 'god of this age' in the sense of holding usurped influence over a fallen world (2 Cor 4:4), and Psalm 115:16 refers to divinely delegated stewardship, not ownership transfer. On that reading, God retains absolute title while humanity and Satan hold derivative or illegitimate sway. That's coherent systematic theology, but it only works if you accept the later canonical framework of usurpation-and-delegation that develops in intertestamental and New Testament thought. The temptation narrative in Matthew and Luke depends on Satan having real authority to offer — Jesus does not rebuke the offer as illegitimate, he rejects it on worship grounds, which implicitly concedes Satan could deliver. Meanwhile the Hebrew Bible's affirmations of Yahweh's ownership have no counterpart conception of a cosmic rival holding usurped title; that dualism is a Second Temple development visible in Qumran's War Scroll, Enochic literature, and then the Synoptic temptation narratives. John Collins and Paula Fredriksen both trace the evolution from Israelite Yahwism's uncontested divine sovereignty to the late-Second-Temple cosmology where Satan operates as a functional rival. So the contradiction isn't logical — it's developmental. The Bible's theology of who owns the earth changed over time, and the final canon preserves snapshots from multiple stages. Psalm 115:16 is a third data point showing that even within the Yahwist tradition there's a minor human-stewardship theme that sits uneasily with the absolute-ownership claims elsewhere.
entries.scholarship: Collins, John J. The Apocalyptic Imagination, 3rd ed. (Eerdmans, 2016), on Second Temple cosmic dualism and evil (esp. the Enoch and Qumran chapters). Fredriksen, Paula. Sin: The Early History of an Idea (Princeton, 2012), on Second Temple developments in the theology of sin and the demonic. Wright, Archie T. The Origin of Evil Spirits (Mohr Siebeck, 2005). Levenson, Jon D. Creation and the Persistence of Evil (Princeton, 1988). Luz, Ulrich. Matthew 1-7, Hermeneia (Fortress, 2007), on Matt 4:8-9. Bock, Darrell L. Luke 1:1-9:50, BECNT (Baker, 1994), on Luke 4:5-6.

entries.question: How long was the Egyptian Captivity?
entries.summary: The Bible gives three different answers to how long Israel was in Egypt: 400 years in Genesis 15:13 and Acts 7:6, four generations in Genesis 15:16, and 430 years in Exodus 12:40 and Galatians 3:17. Even inside a single chapter (Genesis 15), the numbers don't line up, and the New Testament inherits the mess.
entries.commentary: Apologists like Gleason Archer and Kenneth Kitchen try to smooth this out by treating 400 as a round number for 430, and by reading "four generations" as a generic label rather than literal fathers-to-sons counting — especially since biblical "generations" can stretch toward a century in patriarchal chronology. That works as arithmetic gymnastics, but it collapses once you track the actual genealogy. Exodus 6:16-20 gives Levi → Kohath → Amram → Moses, which is exactly four generations, and Kohath is already alive going into Egypt (Genesis 46:11), so those four generations have to cover the entire sojourn. That can't stretch to 430 years without handing Amram a lifespan that makes him a patriarch in his own right. Critical scholarship treats Genesis 15:13-16 as a composite text with two independent chronological traditions stitched together, and Exodus 12:40 itself has competing textual witnesses — the Samaritan Pentateuch and the Septuagint read the 430 years as covering Canaan AND Egypt, cutting the Egyptian stay roughly in half. Paul in Galatians 3:17 is running on that same tradition, counting 430 years from the promise to Sinai, not from the descent into Egypt. So the "contradiction" isn't a simple numerical slip — it's three overlapping sources with three incompatible chronologies, and the New Testament writers picking whichever one served the argument.

Baden, *The Composition of the Pentateuch: Renewing the Documentary Hypothesis* (Yale University Press, 2012). Emanuel Tov, *Textual Criticism of the Hebrew Bible*, 3rd ed. (Fortress, 2012) on Samaritan Pentateuch and LXX variants at Exod 12:40. Gleason L. Archer, *Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties* (Zondervan, 1982), on Exod 12:40 and Gen 15. Kenneth A. Kitchen, *On the Reliability of the Old Testament* (Eerdmans, 2003).

entries.question: What are the borders of Israel?
entries.summary: The Bible draws the borders of the Promised Land at least three different ways. Genesis 15:18 and Exodus 23:31 stretch from the river of Egypt to the Euphrates; Numbers 34 carves out a much smaller box basically the size of Canaan; and Ezekiel 47 draws a third map with Damascus on the northern edge and the Dead Sea region to the south. These aren't the same territory.
entries.commentary: The standard apologetic move — you'll see it in Archer's *Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties* and Walton's *NIV Application Commentary* — is to call Genesis 15 the "ideal" or "maximal" grant that was briefly realized under David and Solomon, and to treat Numbers 34 as the practical tribal allotment. That's a clean story, except the texts don't present themselves that way. Genesis 15:18 uses the language of an unconditional covenant grant, not an aspirational maximum, and 1 Kings 4:21 only describes a sphere of tribute, not occupation to the Euphrates. Critical scholarship reads these as three different border traditions from three different eras and sources: the Genesis 15 grant reflects a Davidic-era imperial horizon, P's Numbers 34 reflects a post-exilic reconstruction of the "true" Canaan, and Ezekiel 47 is the prophet's programmatic vision for a restored, idealized Israel after the exile. Each text is coherent on its own terms; they just don't describe the same land. Treating them as three snapshots of one covenant grant is a harmonization that flattens the compositional layers. More interesting — none of these borders actually matches what Israel or Judah ever controlled archaeologically, which is a separate problem for the historicity of the promise itself.

Block, *The Book of Ezekiel, Chapters 25-48* (NICOT; Eerdmans, 1998), on Ezek 47-48. Moshe Weinfeld, *The Promise of the Land: The Inheritance of the Land of Canaan by the Israelites* (University of California Press, 1993). John H. Walton, *Genesis* (NIV Application Commentary; Zondervan, 2001).

entries.question: How many sons did Abraham have?
entries.summary: Genesis 22:2 calls Isaac Abraham's "only son" — at the moment when Ishmael is already thirteen years old and demonstrably alive, and when Genesis 25 is about to list six more sons by Keturah. So either Abraham has one son, or two, or eight, depending on the page.
entries.commentary: The standard harmonization here — Hamilton in NICOT, Mathews in NAC, and Waltke in *Genesis: A Commentary* all run this play — is that "only son" in Genesis 22:2 is shorthand for "only son of the covenant promise," with Ishmael having been formally cut out by Genesis 21 and the Keturah sons chronologically later. That's a coherent theological reading, and the Hebrew *yachid* does get used elsewhere in the sense of "favored" or "unique" (Zech 12:10, Ps 22:20). But it papers over a real tension: Genesis 22:2 piles up the language — "your son, your only son, whom you love, Isaac" — in a way that reads as emphatic *literal* status, not as a covenant qualifier. James Kugel and Joel Baden point out that the Akedah (Genesis 22) in its source-critical layer almost certainly didn't know about the Ishmael material — the story reads as if Isaac is Abraham's singular child, full stop. When the redactor stitched the cycles together, the Ishmael tradition created exactly this kind of surface contradiction. Acts 7:8 and Hebrews 11:17 both inherit the "only son" framing uncritically, which tells you the tension was already baked in by the time Second Temple readers got hold of it. The apologetic reading saves the theology; it doesn't save the arithmetic.
entries.scholarship: Victor P. Hamilton, *The Book of Genesis, Chapters 18-50* (NICOT; Eerdmans, 1995), on Gen 22:2. Kenneth A. Mathews, *Genesis 11:27-50:26* (New American Commentary 1B; B&H, 2005). Bruce K. Waltke with Cathi J. Fredricks, *Genesis: A Commentary* (Zondervan, 2001). James L. Kugel, *How to Read the Bible: A Guide to Scripture, Then and Now* (Free Press, 2007). Joel S. Baden, *The Composition of the Pentateuch* (Yale University Press, 2012). Jon D. Levenson, *The Death and Resurrection of the Beloved Son* (Yale University Press, 1993).

entries.question: Is circumcision required?
entries.books_in_tension: Genesis, Leviticus, Luke, Acts, 1 Corinthians, Galatians, Colossians
entries.summary: Genesis 17 makes circumcision an "everlasting covenant" — every male, slave or free, on the eighth day, no exceptions. Paul in Galatians 5:2-4 says if you get circumcised, "Christ shall profit you nothing" and you are "fallen from grace." One text treats the uncircumcised as covenant-breakers; the other treats the circumcised as grace-losers.
entries.commentary: The standard Christian harmonization — you'll find it in Schreiner's BECNT Galatians and Moo's commentary on the same letter — is that circumcision was a provisional sign for the old covenant, fulfilled and superseded in Christ, so the Genesis 17 "everlasting" language gets read as everlasting-within-its-dispensation. That's dispensational theology doing real work. The problem is that the Hebrew *berit olam* in Genesis 17:13 is the same phrase used for the Sabbath (Exod 31:16) and for the Davidic covenant (2 Sam 23:5), and nobody argues those expired. Critical scholarship reads this exactly the way it looks: Paul is an apocalyptic Jewish reformer who decided, on the basis of his Christ experience, that the gentile mission required dropping the ethnic-identity markers — and in doing so he directly contradicted Torah. E. P. Sanders, Paula Fredriksen, and James Dunn have all documented this as a major rupture, not a smooth continuity. Acts 16:3 makes it messier, not cleaner — Paul *does* circumcise Timothy, which either means he pragmatically bent his own rule or Acts is projecting a later, more accommodating Paul backwards. Luke 2:21 is irrelevant to the contradiction; Jesus was circumcised as a Jew under Torah. The real tension is Genesis 17 vs. Galatians 5, and it's not a tension — it's a repudiation.
entries.scholarship: Thomas R. Schreiner, *Galatians* (Zondervan Exegetical Commentary on the New Testament; Zondervan, 2010). Douglas J. Moo, *Galatians* (BECNT; Baker Academic, 2013). E. P. Sanders, *Paul, the Law, and the Jewish People* (Fortress, 1983). Paula Fredriksen, *Paul: The Pagan's Apostle* (Yale University Press, 2017). James D. G. Dunn, *The Theology of Paul the Apostle* (Eerdmans, 1998). John J. Collins, *The Invention of Judaism: Torah and Jewish Identity from Deuteronomy to Paul* (University of California Press, 2017).

entries.question: Is incest forbidden?
entries.summary: Leviticus 18 and 20 and Deuteronomy 27 explicitly criminalize sex between half-siblings who share a father — it's called "a wicked thing" and draws a curse. Genesis 20:12 has Abraham calmly explain that Sarah is his half-sister on his father's side and also his wife, and God blesses the marriage in Genesis 17:16. Either the Torah's incest code applies to the patriarchs or it doesn't.
entries.commentary: Apologists like Archer and Walton run two different harmonizations here, and they don't combine well. The first move is chronological: the Levitical code hadn't been given yet in Abraham's time, so he wasn't under it. The second move is textual: maybe "sister" in Genesis 20:12 means something looser, like cousin or clanswoman, and Abraham was fudging to protect himself from Pharaoh. Pick one — they pull in opposite directions. The chronological defense concedes the contradiction in principle (Abraham would have been breaking the later law if it applied) and just pushes it behind a dispensational wall. The "loose sister" defense has to explain why Genesis 20:12 goes out of its way to specify "the daughter of my father, but not the daughter of my mother" — that level of precision is the exact half-sister relationship Leviticus 18:9 explicitly forbids. Critical scholarship treats this as obvious: the patriarchal narratives preserve older legal and social norms (sister-wife marriage is attested in ancient Near Eastern royal houses), and the Levitical and Deuteronomic codes reflect later priestly and Deuteronomic systematization. The contradiction is real; the harmonization requires you to both admit and deny that Torah applies to the patriarchs in the same breath.
entries.scholarship: Jacob Milgrom, *Leviticus 17-22* (Anchor Bible 3A; Doubleday, 2000), on Lev 18:9. Nahum M. Sarna, *Genesis* (JPS Torah Commentary; Jewish Publication Society, 1989). Walton, *Genesis* (NIV Application Commentary; Zondervan, 2001). Gordon J. Wenham, *Genesis 16-50* (Word Biblical Commentary 2; Word, 1994).

entries.question: Did Sarah have faith that she would conceive?
entries.summary: Hebrews 11:11 puts Sarah in the faith hall of fame — "through faith also Sara herself received strength to conceive." Genesis 18:10-15 shows Sarah laughing at the promise, getting caught laughing, and then lying about having laughed. Those are not the same Sarah.
entries.commentary: Apologists like F. F. Bruce and Peter O'Brien's predecessors in Hebrews scholarship (and Cockerill in the current NICNT Hebrews) work hard to rescue Hebrews 11:11 by noting a textual and grammatical tangle: the Greek is awkward enough that some read the verse as actually about *Abraham* receiving power to beget, with Sarah mentioned only as the recipient — which would dodge the contradiction entirely. That's a live exegetical option, and Bruce Metzger's textual commentary flags the issue. But the majority reading, and the one Hebrews' author clearly intended within his broader rhetorical pattern, is that Sarah is the subject of faith in that verse. Under the majority reading, the contradiction is direct: Genesis paints a woman who explicitly disbelieves the promise ("after I am waxed old shall I have pleasure") and then lies to an omniscient God about her reaction. Hebrews retrofits that same woman into an exemplar of faith. Craig Koester and Luke Timothy Johnson both describe this as Hebrews doing midrashic rehabilitation of the patriarchal narratives — a common Second Temple Jewish move where flawed figures get sanitized for homiletic use. The contradiction isn't between two equally literal accounts; it's between a narrative and a later theological reframing that papers over the narrative. That's post-hoc rationalization, not harmonization.
entries.scholarship: Craig R. Koester, *Hebrews* (Anchor Yale Bible 36; Yale University Press, 2001), on Heb 11:11. Gareth Lee Cockerill, *The Epistle to the Hebrews* (NICNT; Eerdmans, 2012). Luke Timothy Johnson, *Hebrews: A Commentary* (New Testament Library; Westminster John Knox, 2006). Bruce M. Metzger, *A Textual Commentary on the Greek New Testament*, 2nd ed. (United Bible Societies, 1994), on Heb 11:11. Harold W. Attridge, *The Epistle to the Hebrews* (Hermeneia; Fortress, 1989). Nahum M. Sarna, *Genesis* (JPS Torah Commentary; Jewish Publication Society, 1989).

entries.question: Can God do anything?
entries.summary: Genesis 18:14 asks the rhetorical question "Is any thing too hard for the LORD?" — the obvious answer being no. Judges 1:19 then says Yahweh was with Judah and "drave out the inhabitants of the mountain; but could not drive out the inhabitants of the valley, because they had chariots of iron." Apparently iron chariots were too hard for the LORD.
entries.commentary: The standard apologetic move — Archer pushes this one, and so does the NIV Study Bible footnote — is that the Hebrew in Judges 1:19 is ambiguous about the subject: maybe it was Judah who couldn't drive them out, not Yahweh, and the Lord's presence isn't the agent of the failure. That reading is grammatically defensible. But it runs into a bigger problem: elsewhere the text is perfectly comfortable saying God couldn't deliver on his own side of a battle. Deuteronomy 7 promises God will drive out the Canaanites entirely; Joshua 17:16-18 has Joshua telling Ephraim they'll have trouble precisely because of iron chariots; and Jeremiah 32:17 reaffirms "nothing is too hard for thee." So even if you grant the ambiguous-subject reading of Judges 1:19, the text still has to explain why the outcome — failure to conquer — matches what you'd expect from a limited deity rather than a universal covenant promise. Critical scholars like Mark Smith and Baruch Halpern read these tensions as evidence of Yahweh's evolution from a regional storm/war god with localized power to the later universal deity of Second Isaiah. The "nothing is too hard" rhetoric is the developed theology; the iron-chariot embarrassment is the older, more parochial layer leaking through. The harmonization saves the verse; it doesn't save the theology.

Archer, *Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties* (Zondervan, 1982).

entries.question: Was Lot a righteous man?
entries.summary: 2 Peter 2:7-8 calls Lot "just" and "righteous" and describes his soul as vexed by the wickedness of Sodom. Genesis 19 shows the same Lot offering his virgin daughters to a rape mob and later getting drunk enough on two consecutive nights to impregnate both of them. The narrative and the endorsement don't line up.
entries.commentary: Apologists like Archer and Peter H. Davids (in the PNTC 2 Peter, which is not the withdrawn O'Brien volume) argue that 2 Peter 2 is drawing a *relative* contrast — Lot was righteous compared to the people of Sodom, not righteous in any absolute sense. That's a fair grammatical reading of the Greek *dikaios*, and it matches how Second Temple Jewish retellings (Wisdom of Solomon 10:6, Philo, Josephus) were already rehabilitating Lot's reputation before 2 Peter came along. So the harmonization works as a descriptive claim — yes, ancient readers made this move. But that's exactly the critical point: 2 Peter isn't reading Genesis 19 straight, it's inheriting a reception-history where Lot got progressively scrubbed. Genesis itself doesn't call Lot righteous. Genesis shows a man who prioritizes his male guests over his daughters' bodily safety and then passes out drunk enough to commit incest twice in a row without noticing. James Kugel catalogs the Second Temple rehabilitation machinery in detail — the same move gets run on Noah, on Jacob, on Judah. The contradiction here isn't between Genesis and 2 Peter arbitrarily; it's between what Genesis actually narrates and what later Jewish and Christian tradition needed to say about the patriarchs. Call it what it is: theological retcon.

entries.question: Who destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah?
entries.summary: Genesis 19:13 has the two angels telling Lot, "we will destroy this place ... the LORD hath sent us to destroy it." Eleven verses later, Genesis 19:24 says "the LORD rained upon Sodom and upon Gomorrah brimstone and fire from the LORD out of heaven." So the agent is either the angels, or Yahweh directly, or somehow both — and the text doesn't pick one.
entries.commentary: This one is the mildest contradiction in the batch, and honest apologists handle it easily: the standard harmonization is that the angels are God's agents, so Yahweh destroying the cities *through* the angels and Yahweh destroying them directly amount to the same act. Hamilton and Wenham both frame it that way in their Genesis commentaries. That's fine as a theological reading. The more interesting critical question is what Genesis 19:24 is actually saying with that odd doubled construction — "the LORD rained ... from the LORD out of heaven." Some rabbinic and patristic readers treated that as evidence of two divine figures, which later Christian apologists like Justin Martyr used for proto-trinitarian arguments. Critical scholars like Mark Smith and Benjamin Sommer read it as a relic of older West Semitic theology where multiple manifestations of a deity could be referenced distinctly — the "fluidity of selfhood" Sommer documents in *The Bodies of God*. So the surface contradiction (angels vs. God) dissolves into agency language, but the verse underneath preserves something weirder and older than monotheism would strictly allow. That is of course a subjective opinion on which layer is doing the real work in the verse.

Smith, *The Origins of Biblical Monotheism* (Oxford University Press, 2001).

entries.question: How many generations from Abraham to Moses?
entries.summary: Genesis 15:16 promises Abraham's descendants will return to Canaan "in the fourth generation." But when you actually trace the genealogy Genesis and Exodus give — Abraham → Isaac → Jacob → Levi → Kohath → Amram → Moses — you get six or seven generations depending on how you count, not four.
entries.commentary: Apologists like Archer handle this by treating "generation" (Hebrew *dor*) as a long temporal unit rather than a single father-to-son step — one *dor* could be a century, they argue, so four *dorot* equals the 400 years of Genesis 15:13. That's linguistically defensible; *dor* does have semantic range. The problem is that Exodus itself seems to count the generations literally. Exodus 6:16-20 gives the Levi-Kohath-Amram-Moses chain — that's explicitly four steps from Levi (who went INTO Egypt per Gen 46:11) to Moses (who came out). So the "fourth generation" of Genesis 15:16 either matches the Levi-to-Moses count (four) or the Abraham-to-Moses count (six or seven), but you can't have it both ways with the chronology of Exodus 12:40's 430 years attached. Joel Baden and Richard Elliott Friedman both read this as a classic Documentary Hypothesis seam — the "four generations" tradition comes from one source stratum, the 400/430 year tradition from another, and the genealogical material in Exodus 6 is P's attempt to make it all fit. The numbers don't line up because they were never a unified chronology to begin with. The "dor means century" move is a rescue operation that requires ignoring what Exodus 6 is actually doing.

entries.question: How old was Ishmael when he was abandoned by Abraham?
entries.summary: Genesis 21:14-18 describes Hagar carrying Ishmael on her shoulder, laying "the child" under a shrub, and being told to lift up "the lad" — infant language. But Genesis 17:24-25 plus Genesis 21:5-9 has Ishmael at thirteen when circumcised and Isaac weaned (age 2-3) before the abandonment scene, which puts Ishmael somewhere between 14 and 17 years old. A teenager doesn't ride on the shoulder.
entries.commentary: Apologists like Mathews in NAC and Hamilton in NICOT try to resolve this by retranslating Genesis 21:14: the Hebrew may be saying Abraham placed the bread and water on Hagar's shoulder, and *then separately* gave her the child — not that the child was on her shoulder. That's grammatically plausible; the Masoretic syntax is ambiguous enough to allow it, and NRSV and NIV both render it that way. Fair enough. But that rescue only handles the shoulder detail. It doesn't explain why Hagar "casts" Ishmael under a bush (21:15), why the narrative keeps calling him *yeled* ("child") and treating him as physically helpless while Hagar weeps over him, or why the angel tells Hagar to "lift up the lad" — all language that reads naturally for a toddler and awkwardly for a mid-teen. Critical scholars like Baden, Friedman, and Westermann read Genesis 21 as coming from E, while the chronological markers in Genesis 17 and 21:5 come from P. The two sources had different pictures of Ishmael's age at this moment and the redactor didn't smooth them out. The harmonization works at the level of individual words; it doesn't work at the level of the scene's whole texture.

Sarna, *Genesis* (JPS Torah Commentary; Jewish Publication Society, 1989).

entries.question: Is it OK to swear?
entries.summary: Deuteronomy 6:13, Isaiah 65:16, and Jeremiah 4:2 and 12:16 all positively command swearing by Yahweh's name. Matthew 5:34-37 has Jesus saying "swear not at all" — no heaven, no earth, just yes-yes and no-no, and anything more "cometh of evil." Torah makes oaths by God's name an act of covenantal loyalty; Jesus makes them a moral problem.
entries.commentary: The standard apologetic — D. A. Carson runs this in his Matthew commentary, and Craig Blomberg takes the same line — is that Jesus isn't abolishing oaths per se, he's forbidding the casuistic abuse of oaths that first-century Jewish legal culture had developed, where you could swear by "Jerusalem" or "your head" to sound binding without actually being legally bound. Matthew 23:16-22 supports this reading: Jesus condemns the "you swear by the temple, it's nothing, but swear by the gold of the temple, you're bound" system. Fair. But the Sermon on the Mount formula is categorical — "swear not at all" — and the Epistle of James 5:12 repeats it just as categorically. Early Christian groups (the Anabaptists, the Quakers) read this as a straight prohibition for centuries, and they weren't wrong about the plain sense. Dale Allison and W. D. Davies in their ICC Matthew argue Jesus is radicalizing Torah here in the same pattern as the other antitheses in Matthew 5 — taking a Torah allowance (oaths by the Name) and canceling it under the inbreaking kingdom. That's a genuine contradiction with Deuteronomy 6:13, not a casuistic footnote. The harmonization works if you allow Jesus to be selectively overriding Torah; it just doesn't work if you need the Old Testament and Jesus to be saying the same thing.

Carson, *Matthew* (Expositor's Bible Commentary; Zondervan, 1984). Craig L. Blomberg, *Matthew* (New American Commentary 22; B&H, 1992). Ulrich Luz, *Matthew 1-7: A Commentary* (Hermeneia; Fortress, 2007).

entries.question: Has God ever tempted anyone?
entries.summary: James 1:13 draws a hard line: "God cannot be tempted with evil, neither tempteth he any man." Genesis 22:1 opens the Akedah by saying "God did tempt Abraham" and tells him to sacrifice Isaac. The KJV translates the same Hebrew and Greek roots consistently, which is why this reads as a contradiction in English.
entries.commentary: Apologists like Archer, Wenham, and Douglas Moo in his James commentary resolve this through translation: the Hebrew verb *nissah* in Genesis 22:1 means "test" or "prove," not "tempt" in the James 1:13 sense of luring toward evil. Modern translations (NIV, NRSV, ESV) render Genesis 22:1 as "tested" precisely to dodge the semantic collision. That's a legitimate philological point — *nissah* and the Greek *peirazō* in James 1:13 overlap but aren't identical, and James is clearly talking about enticement toward sin, while Genesis 22 is a loyalty test. So in modern translation the contradiction softens. BUT — and this is the critical wrinkle — the KJV reading isn't wrong, it's just old. The underlying theological problem doesn't go away: whether you call it "testing" or "tempting," God is in Genesis 22 deliberately commanding Abraham to commit what Torah elsewhere defines as abomination (human sacrifice, Lev 18:21, Deut 12:31). James 1:13 says God "cannot be tempted with evil" — but Genesis 22 has God commanding evil as a loyalty check. Jon Levenson's *The Death and Resurrection of the Beloved Son* digs into how uncomfortable this made ancient interpreters, who went to enormous lengths (LXX renderings, Jubilees 17-18 blaming Mastema/Satan for the prompt) to get God out of directly initiating the test. The translation fix saves the verses; it doesn't save the theological problem.
entries.scholarship: Douglas J. Moo, *The Letter of James* (Pillar New Testament Commentary; Eerdmans, 2000). Gordon J. Wenham, *Genesis 16-50* (Word Biblical Commentary 2; Word, 1994), on Gen 22:1. Archer, *Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties* (Zondervan, 1982).

entries.question: Does God approve of human sacrifice?
entries.summary: Leviticus 18:21, Deuteronomy 12:31, and 2 Kings 21:6 condemn making your child pass through the fire as abomination. Genesis 22:2 has Yahweh himself commanding Abraham to offer Isaac as a burnt offering on a mountain. Torah says human sacrifice is what the nations do that Yahweh hates; Genesis has Yahweh ordering it.
entries.commentary: The standard apologetic move — Walton, Archer, and Copan in *Is God a Moral Monster?* all run this one — is that the Akedah is a test God never intended to let go through; the ram is provided, Isaac lives, and the episode actually functions as a *polemic against* human sacrifice, demonstrating that Yahweh is different from the Molech-worshipers because he stops the knife. That's a real reading and it's theologically useful. But it's not watertight. First, the command itself is unambiguous — "offer him there for a burnt offering" — and Abraham's willingness, not his refusal, is what the text praises. Second, Jephthah's daughter in Judges 11 gets actually sacrificed with no narrative condemnation and with the text straightforwardly reporting that Jephthah "did with her according to his vow." Third, critical scholars like Jon Levenson and Francesca Stavrakopoulou have documented substantial evidence that child sacrifice was practiced in pre-exilic Israelite religion (the *molek* offerings, the Hinnom valley cult), and that the Torah's repeated prohibitions are polemics against a practice that was demonstrably internal to Israel, not just foreign. Ezekiel 20:25-26 even has Yahweh admitting to giving Israel "statutes that were not good" involving the offering of firstborns as a punishment. The Akedah either sits awkwardly with that history or reflects an earlier theological layer where the question of whether Yahweh wanted human sacrifice wasn't as settled as Leviticus wants it to be. Take your pick; neither option lets the apologetic "polemic against sacrifice" reading stand unchallenged.
entries.scholarship: Jon D. Levenson, *The Death and Resurrection of the Beloved Son* (Yale University Press, 1993). Francesca Stavrakopoulou, *King Manasseh and Child Sacrifice: Biblical Distortions of Historical Realities* (BZAW 338; de Gruyter, 2004). Jacob Milgrom, *Leviticus 17-22* (Anchor Bible 3A; Doubleday, 2000). Paul Copan, *Is God a Moral Monster? Making Sense of the Old Testament God* (Baker Books, 2011). John H. Walton, *Genesis* (NIV Application Commentary; Zondervan, 2001). Susan Niditch, *War in the Hebrew Bible: A Study in the Ethics of Violence* (Oxford University Press, 1993).

entries.question: Was Keturah Abraham's wife or concubine?
entries.summary: Genesis 25:1 says "then again Abraham took a wife, and her name was Keturah." 1 Chronicles 1:32 calls her "Abraham's concubine." In biblical Hebrew those are two different legal statuses, and the Chronicler is demoting what Genesis promoted.
entries.commentary: Apologists like Archer and Mathews typically handle this by noting that ancient Hebrew status terminology isn't as rigid as modern legal categories — a *pilegesh* (concubine) could be a secondary wife with limited inheritance rights, and the same woman could be called both "wife" (*ishshah*) and "concubine" depending on context and genealogical purpose. Genesis 25:6 actually speaks of Abraham's "concubines" in the plural when sending away the sons of Keturah with gifts, while keeping Isaac as the heir, so even Genesis itself flickers on her status. That softens the contradiction. But the critical point Sara Japhet makes in her I & II Chronicles commentary is that the Chronicler is doing *deliberate* editorial work on the patriarchal genealogies — cleaning up lineage status, consolidating tribes, making succession lines explicit. Calling Keturah a concubine rather than a wife is part of the Chronicler's systematic move to elevate Isaac's Sarah-descent as the exclusive legitimate line and downgrade Abraham's other wives and their sons to lower-status branches. So the "contradiction" is real at the lexical level, and it's not an accident. It's the Chronicler rewriting the Genesis record to match a later theological hierarchy. That's a small contradiction with a big implication about how scripture edits itself.

Mathews, *Genesis 11:27-50:26* (New American Commentary 1B; B&H, 2005). Gordon J. Wenham, *Genesis 16-50* (Word Biblical Commentary 2; Word, 1994). Nahum M. Sarna, *Genesis* (JPS Torah Commentary; Jewish Publication Society, 1989). Gary N. Knoppers, *I Chronicles 1-9* (Anchor Bible 12; Doubleday, 2003).

assessment.reasoning: The flexible pilegesh/ishshah terminology (and Gen 25:6's plural 'concubines') softens the lexical clash, but Japhet shows the Chronicler is deliberately demoting Keturah to fit a later genealogical hierarchy, making this a real if minor editorial contradiction.

entries.question: What is the human life span?
entries.summary: Psalm 90:10 puts the human lifespan at seventy years. Genesis 6:3 has Yahweh cap it at 120 years. The patriarchal genealogies then list people who live 950 (Noah), 600 (Shem), 464 (Eber), and 175 (Abraham) — blowing past both numbers by orders of magnitude. The Bible gives you three incompatible answers.
entries.commentary: Apologists handle this three different ways depending on which tradition they're defending. Young-earth creationists like Henry Morris argue the antediluvian lifespans were literal and the post-flood drop reflects environmental collapse (the vapor canopy theory — which has no scientific support). Archer and Walton take the softer line: the Genesis 6:3 "120 years" is a promise of impending judgment (the flood comes in 120 years), not a cap on human lifespan, and Psalm 90:10 is poetic observation, not a decree. That's a coherent reading of Genesis 6:3 in context, and it's probably the best apologetic option. But it still leaves the core issue that the patriarchal numbers sit in their own chronological universe. Critical scholarship — John Walton's own *Ancient Near Eastern Thought* included — recognizes the Genesis 5 and 11 lifespan lists as stylized, theologically freighted numbers paralleling the Sumerian King List, where antediluvian kings reigned tens of thousands of years before the numbers shrink post-flood. They're doing genre work, not biology. Psalm 90 is doing something else — wisdom literature reflecting on human finitude. The "contradiction" is real when you treat all three as modern-style factual claims about the same topic; it dissolves when you recognize they're three different genres doing three different rhetorical jobs. But that recognition is itself a concession that the Bible doesn't speak univocally on human lifespan.
entries.scholarship: Victor P. Hamilton, *The Book of Genesis, Chapters 1-17* (NICOT; Eerdmans, 1990). Kenneth A. Mathews, *Genesis 1-11:26* (New American Commentary 1A; B&H, 1996). entries.question: Will there be many Jews?
entries.summary: Genesis 22:17-18 and 26:4 promise Abraham's and Isaac's descendants will be as numerous as the stars of heaven and the sand on the shore. Deuteronomy 4:23-27 threatens that if they make a graven image, Yahweh will scatter them and leave them "few in number among the heathen." One promise is unconditional multiplication; the other is conditional reduction.
entries.commentary: The apologetic move here is straightforward and pretty solid: the two verses operate at different covenant levels. Genesis 22 is the Abrahamic covenant, which scripture treats as unconditional; Deuteronomy 4 is the Mosaic covenant, which is explicitly conditional on obedience. Paul even makes this distinction load-bearing in Galatians 3. That's a coherent distinction and it holds. But the critical question is whether the two covenants really sit together the way the apologetic framework claims. Deuteronomy 4:31 immediately pulls back from the scattering threat by invoking the Abrahamic covenant ("he will not forget the covenant of thy fathers"), which means the Deuteronomist himself thought the two promises needed reconciliation — and he did it by having the Abrahamic one eventually override the Mosaic threat. That's not a clean two-covenant system; that's a post-exilic theologian trying to explain why the exile happened while preserving the "many descendants" promise. Critical scholars like Moshe Weinfeld and Bernard Levinson read Deuteronomy as a deliberate revision of earlier covenant theology — updating the unconditional patriarchal promises to include conditional threats as a response to the actual historical catastrophe of the northern kingdom's fall. So the "contradiction" is also a record of theology evolving in real time to handle real events. Calling it a simple two-covenant system papers over what the text is doing historically.

Block, *Deuteronomy* (NIV Application Commentary; Zondervan, 2012).

entries.question: Who named Beersheba?
entries.summary: Genesis 21:31 has Abraham naming Beersheba after his well-treaty with Abimelech. Genesis 26:33 has Isaac naming the same place, after his own well-treaty with a Philistine king also named Abimelech, with the narrator noting "therefore the name of the city is Beersheba unto this day" — as if the name originated there.
entries.commentary: Apologists like Hamilton and Waltke handle this with the "re-naming" or "re-digging" solution: both Abraham and Isaac had well disputes with Abimelech at the same site, Isaac's wells were re-dug over his father's (explicit in Gen 26:18), and he re-applied the existing name in a commemorative ceremony. That's workable as narrative logic. But it doesn't handle the problem that both accounts use "therefore" / etiological-origin language — each text presents itself as the *first* explanation for the name. And the two stories are suspiciously parallel beyond the naming: Abraham pretends Sarah is his sister to Abimelech (Gen 20), Isaac pretends Rebekah is his sister to Abimelech (Gen 26), both cut a treaty at Beersheba with officials named Phicol, both dig or claim wells. Critical scholarship — Gunkel long ago, and more recently Friedman, Baden, and Ronald Hendel — reads these as two variants of a single traditional legend attached to both patriarchs independently in the oral tradition and then preserved as two separate narratives when the sources were written down and combined. That's the classic "doublet" phenomenon. Treating them as two distinct historical events at the same spot with the same kind of king is possible, but the odds of that much coincidence are what the Documentary Hypothesis was designed to explain. The harmonization technically works; it just costs more than the source-critical explanation.
entries.scholarship: Victor P. Hamilton, *The Book of Genesis, Chapters 18-50* (NICOT; Eerdmans, 1995). Bruce K. Waltke with Cathi J. Fredricks, *Genesis: A Commentary* (Zondervan, 2001). Hermann Gunkel, *Genesis*, trans. Mark E. Biddle (Mercer University Press, 1997; German orig. 1901). Richard Elliott Friedman, *The Bible with Sources Revealed* (HarperOne, 2003). Joel S. Baden, *The Composition of the Pentateuch* (Yale University Press, 2012). Ronald S. Hendel, *Remembering Abraham: Culture, Memory, and History in the Hebrew Bible* (Oxford University Press, 2005).

entries.question: Who was Laban's father?
entries.summary: Genesis 28:5 explicitly identifies Laban as "the son of Bethuel the Syrian." Genesis 29:5 has Jacob asking shepherds, "Know ye Laban the son of Nahor?" Bethuel and Nahor are not the same person — Nahor is Bethuel's father and Laban's grandfather in Genesis 22:20-23.
entries.commentary: Apologists like Archer and Mathews handle this with the ancient Near Eastern "son of" convention: *ben* in Hebrew can mean son, grandson, or descendant generally, and Genesis 29:5's "son of Nahor" just means Laban belongs to the Nahorite family line, with Nahor as the identifiable clan patriarch. That's philologically defensible — Matthew 1:1 calls Jesus "son of David, son of Abraham" in exactly the same extended sense. The apologetic reading works. What it doesn't quite handle is why the narrator switches conventions between Genesis 28:5 (strict biological "son of Bethuel") and Genesis 29:5 (loose genealogical "son of Nahor") within the space of a few verses, with no narrative signal that a different sense is in play. Critical scholars like Friedman and Westermann note that this is one of many small signs of source-combination in the Jacob cycle: the patriarchal narratives preserve multiple oral traditions about the same figures, and the grandfather-vs-father variation reflects genuinely different genealogical traditions rather than a consistent use of "son" as "descendant." So the apologetic explanation is live — "son of" really can mean descendant — it just has to assume the narrator is inconsistent within a single pericope for no rhetorical reason. The source-critical explanation accounts for the inconsistency without requiring that assumption. Parsimony favors the latter.
entries.scholarship: Victor P. Hamilton, *The Book of Genesis, Chapters 18-50* (NICOT; Eerdmans, 1995). Kenneth A. Mathews, *Genesis 11:27-50:26* (New American Commentary 1B; B&H, 2005). Claus Westermann, *Genesis 12-36: A Commentary* (Augsburg, 1985). Richard Elliott Friedman, *The Bible with Sources Revealed* (HarperOne, 2003). Nahum M. Sarna, *Genesis* (JPS Torah Commentary; Jewish Publication Society, 1989). Gleason L. Archer, *Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties* (Zondervan, 1982).
